The coffin is placed in the East Room. Robert Kennedy looks at the body and asks Bill Walton's view; Walton says it looks like a wax dummy, and the family keeps the casket closed. Schlesinger and Mrs. Kennedy also say it did not look like him (per Manchester).
Robert Kennedy takes a sleeping pill in the Lincoln bedroom; Charles Spalding hears him sobbing, asking God why.
Klein's identifies Oswald (as "A. Hidell") as the buyer of rifle C2766.
FBI agent Drain reaches Washington with the rifle.

Soon after waking, Johnson has Kennedy's secretary Evelyn Lincoln told to clear her desk that morning and Kennedy's effects, including his rocking chair, removed. He declares Monday a national day of mourning.

The Dallas Morning News quotes DA Wade saying early reports suggest more than one person was involved. Johnson aide Cliff Carter phones Wade three times to say talk of a foreign conspiracy would shake the nation. In New Orleans, lawyer Dean Andrews says from his hospital bed that a "Clay Bertrand" asked him to represent Oswald.
Johnson asks Pierre Salinger to stay on as press secretary; Salinger agrees.
Emory Roberts's shift, the agents from the Dallas follow-up car, reports early to the Elms and is told to be careful with weapons.
A .38 Smith & Wesson revolver in a paper sack is turned in to Dallas police, found near Ross and Lamar several blocks from Dealey Plaza. The FBI investigates it, but no conclusion is recorded.
Robert Kennedy walks alone on the South Grounds.
Life's Richard Stolley views the Zapruder film with Zapruder, Secret Service agents present.
Secret Service report: the limousine guard changes; at 4 PM Protective Research staff photograph the car, and at 4:30 the debris is removed from its floor and the special guard ends.
The FBI receives Kennedy's clothing from the Secret Service.
Johnson arrives at the White House for his first intelligence briefing in the Situation Room.
CIA director McCone speaks with Robert Kennedy before meeting Johnson.
The Secret Service shows the Zapruder film at Zapruder's office to a few reporters, including Dan Rather.
Two Life reporters take Marina and Marguerite Oswald and the children from the Paine house to the Adolphus Hotel. Ted Kennedy tells his father of the death.
Robert Kennedy finds Evelyn Lincoln in tears outside the Oval Office, told to be out by 9:30.

A stranger claiming to be Adrian Alba's friend browses the gun magazines at Alba's New Orleans garage, where Oswald used to read them. Later an American Rifleman from the garage bearing Oswald's thumbprint has a Klein's coupon torn out matching one in Oswald's effects.
But Klein's records say the rifle was ordered from the February issue, not that June issue, and the stranger's visit taints the magazine evidence.

McCone briefs Johnson on Oswald's Mexico City contacts, including a Soviet vice consul the CIA believes is a KGB assassinations specialist, raising the possibility of a foreign plot and that Oswald might be killed before talking.
Life buys print rights to the Zapruder film for $50,000 and takes the "original"; it later pays $150,000 for all rights.
Ford's F. Vaughan Ferguson inspects only the limousine's windshield, finds cracks but no hole, and is told to arrange a replacement.
Hoover tells Johnson the case against Oswald is "not very, very strong" and wrongly places the shooting on the fifth floor; a written report later corrects him.
The recording of this call is reported to have a 14-minute gap, or to have been replaced with a blank belt; Johnson's diary records the call.
Oswald is brought to Fritz's office for interrogation.
Mrs. Kennedy brings her children into the East Room for a few minutes alone with the casket.
Chief Curry says FBI agents had interviewed Oswald and knew his activities; Hoover has Shanklin demand a retraction, and Curry gives one.
Oswald is returned to his cell.
Carousel Club handyman Larry Crafard leaves Dallas without a word and hitchhikes to Michigan with $7; the FBI finds him days later.

Ruby parks and walks to City Hall. In Houston, Ferrie tells the FBI he spent two hours at the Winterland rink discussing the business; the owner says Ferrie never skated or discussed costs, only used the pay phone. Ferrie's group visits another rink without skating, goes on to Galveston, and Ferrie calls Marcello's office first.

A mailman gives a WFAA cameraman a 30.06 cartridge he says he found in bushes by the Depository; it sits on reporter Bert Shipp's desk for months before police take it and return it. There are no bushes below the window, and a 30.06 round cannot be fired from the Carcano; the casing is stamped as 1941 Frankford Arsenal military ammunition.
Dallas leaders react: publisher Joe Dealey calls it a tormented town; the mayor is under guard; H.L. Hunt issues a statement; a labor leader calls Dallas a sick city conditioned by hate.
Reporter Ike Pappas recalls chaos and no special passes on the third floor of police headquarters. Gilberto Policarpo Lopez crosses into Mexico at Laredo; he flies to Cuba four days later.

An FBI memo to the Secret Service says Dallas agents who spoke with Oswald listened to the Mexico City recording and saw the photograph of the man who called himself Lee Oswald, and believe that man was not Oswald.
The State Department says there is no evidence of Soviet or other foreign involvement; Castro asks why it needed to say so.
France-Soir reporter Philippe Labro meets Ruby at police headquarters.
Robert Oswald visits his brother through glass. Lee warns the line is taped, says he does not know what is going on, and tells Robert not to believe the so-called evidence.

Three people named Mertz fly from Houston to Mexico City; Michel Mertz and Michel Roux are names used as aliases by French ex-officer Jean Souetre, said to have been in Dallas on November 22. A deserter named Michel Roux also travels from Fort Worth to Houston and on to Mexico City.

Houston dentist Dr. Alderson later says FBI agents questioned him in December about his friend Souetre, saying they had traced him to Dallas the day before and lost him; Souetre later denied knowing Alderson. Fritz is said to have later claimed a call from Johnson telling him "You have your man" and to stop investigating.
Deputy Buddy Walthers reports that Oswald had been seen at 3128 Harlandale, where Cubans held weekend meetings, and that the house was vacated around the assassination.
Oklahoma motel manager Jack Zangetty reportedly tells friends three men, not Oswald, killed the President and that a man named Ruby will kill Oswald; he is later found dead in a lake.

UPI's Aline Mosby recalls her 1959 Moscow interview, in which Oswald said he found Das Kapital after moving to North Dakota; the Warren Commission's version of her notes reads "New Orleans," unexplained.
McCone meets Johnson about Oswald's foreign connections.
Oswald is brought back to Fritz's office for questioning.
Oswald is returned to his cell.
Marguerite and Marina Oswald visit him.
At the Nichols garage, attendant Tom Brown hears Ruby on the phone telling someone where Chief Curry is.
Kennedy's rocking chairs are moved out of the White House to the Executive Office Building.
A secret CIA document in Oswald's State Department passport file is destroyed, reportedly by accident, while being copied.
Hoover's memo to Rowley relays the CIA report of a man calling himself Lee Oswald at the Soviet Embassy in Mexico City.
The memo says Dallas agents who heard the tape and saw the photo believe the man was not Oswald; a Belmont memo to Tolson says the same.
Johnson tells lawyer Edwin Weisl the case may have more complications and lie deeper than he thinks.
NBC's Frank McGee reports rain in Washington and so much history so fast.
Johnson calls Marie Tippit with condolences.
Oswald is taken to a fourth lineup. Johnson calls Sen. Smathers about a tax bill.
Johnson holds his first cabinet meeting; Robert Kennedy arrives late and asks for no photographs.
Oswald is returned to his cell after the lineup.
H.L. Hunt is said to meet Jack Crichton and other Army intelligence officers about the first questioning of Marina Oswald.
Stolley hides the Oswald family in a hotel suite for Life. When they offer Oswald's trunk for $10,000 to pay for a lawyer, Life's managing editor refuses to pay the family anything.
Detectives take hair samples from Oswald for the FBI.
The "original" Zapruder film goes to Life's Chicago office; ten black-and-white prints are made.
Fritz announces the case is "cinched" and that Oswald killed the President, without discussing evidence.
Johnson proclaims a period of mourning on television.
Shanklin reports that Dallas labs cannot process the Zapruder film; DeLoach has it flown to Washington for the FBI or a trusted lab.
Hunt security man John Currington later testifies Hunt sent him to check Oswald's jail security; he reported at midnight that there was none to speak of.

Curry tells Shanklin of a North Carolina tip on where the rifle was bought; Belmont soon says the sale was traced to Chicago, and the tip is dropped. That evening Carter again tells Wade to keep foreign conspiracy out of it, and Wade sees Fritz. The CIA's photo center prepares Zapruder enlargements for McCone to show Johnson, tells AMLASH's case officer to break contact, and asks that Sylvia Duran's arrest be called off.

Dan Rather, after a private viewing, describes the film on CBS, saying the head went forward, which he later retracts. Life keeps the film from public view; Zapruder reportedly gives part of his payment to the Tippit family.
On air, Rather tells Hughes Rudd and Richard Hottelet he has just seen a film of the shooting.

Rather describes the car turning onto Elm, Kennedy raising his hand to his face and lurching slightly, Connally turning and being hit, then a shot that drives the President's head forward violently, Mrs. Kennedy climbing onto the trunk, and the car speeding away without stopping.
He says the whole sequence lasts about twenty seconds, the shots no more than five.
Rather says the President was clearly hit twice and Connally once, by an amateur filming from a raised position with his back to the Depository.
Dr. David Mantik notes that after that weekend there is no record of the film being screened until February 1964, time he argues was enough for alterations.
NBC's Nancy Dickerson and her husband dine with the Johnsons at the Elms.
TASS accuses U.S. police of trying to implicate communists and calls the case against Oswald suspicious.

Curry says questioning is over for the day and Oswald will move to the county jail, probably in the morning, telling reporters nothing will happen before 10 AM. Two UPI reporters agree over drinks that someone will try to kill Oswald.
Oswald is returned to his cell, having been questioned less than three hours that day.

Robert Kennedy weeps alone by the casket. Peter Lawford later says RFK believed a plot growing out of a secret anti-Castro operation killed his brother and that the family no longer controlled the government (per Talbot, Brothers).
Ferrie and his friends check into the Driftwood Motel in Galveston; Ferrie stays out until early morning.
A call goes from Ruby's sister's apartment to Ralph Paul's Bullpen restaurant; a waitress recalls Paul discussing a gun on the phone with Ruby.
